links.note: Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). This is Activity 6.7's own table - sugar, salt, chalk, sand and sawdust stirred into water with a prediction column - which is the solubility activity in 32722.

Was 32724 (The Space Water Occupies). The four true/false statements - wood translucent, foil lustrous, sugar dissolves, an apple is matter - are listed verbatim in 32729; only the last touches volume.
Was 32730 (What Recyclers Look For). The chair exercise with its four desirable properties is described in 32729; 32730 is the recycler survey.
Was 32718 (Why a Ball Is Made of What It Is). The conclusion that objects are made up of various materials is Activity 6.1's, in 32715; 32718 is about choosing one for a purpose.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Choice of material by its properties and the object's purpose is 32718's stated rule.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Non-lustrous examples - paper, wood, rubber, jute - are in 32719.
Was 32718 (Why a Ball Is Made of What It Is). Metals dulling under air and moisture is stated in 32719.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Opaque examples - wood, cardboard, metals - are in 32721.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). The hide-and-seek scene with the wall, the tree and the frosted glass door is 32721's own illustration.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Transparent examples - glass, water, air, cellophane - are in 32721.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Lustrous against non-lustrous is the pair 32719 defines.
Was 32717 (Classification Is a Choice of Property). Seeing clearly through a window pane is transparency, 32721; 32717 is the method of grouping, not this property.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Scratching with a metal key is one of the two hardness tests in 32720.
Was 32720 (Hard and Soft Are Relative). Mridu and laghu are two of the twenty gunas listed in 32726; 32720 gives the chapter's own hard/soft test, not the Ayurvedic terms.
Was 32724 (The Space Water Occupies). Anything occupying space and having mass is matter - the definition in 32725; 32724 only establishes volume.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). The earliest Indian pottery and its clay belong to 32716's history note.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). A tumbler's material must be able to hold water - the constraint Activity 6.3 sets in 32718.
Was 32718 (Why a Ball Is Made of What It Is). That one object can be made from different materials is the first result of Activity 6.2, stated in 32717.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Opaque examples are in 32721.
Was 32719 (Lustre). Seen but not clearly is translucent, defined in 32721 with butter paper and frosted glass.
Was 32717 (Classification Is a Choice of Property). Heavier and lighter measured as mass is Activity 6.8's conclusion in 32723.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Material chosen by properties and purpose - 32718's rule.
Was 32718 (Why a Ball Is Made of What It Is). Loss of lustre to air and moisture is stated in 32719.
Was 32717 (Classification Is a Choice of Property). Hardness being relative - rubber harder than sponge, softer than iron - is 32720's qualification.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Lustre with examples, and whether a non-metal can look lustrous, is 32719 - including its all-that-glitters caution about polish and coatings.
Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). Picking a frying-pan material for the job is 32718's property-and-purpose rule applied.

Was 32715 (What Counts as a Material). The surviving statement - that only the cheapest material is chosen - is a claim about how materials are selected, which 32718 governs. Stem is truncated: the numbered statements are missing.
